t: Surrealism aimed, in Breton's words, to resolve the previously contradictory conditions of dream and reality into an absolute reality, a super-reality, and Breton held it to be above all a revolutionary movement.
Two rival groups published manifestos in October 1924, Yvan Goll's on 1 October and Breton's on 15 October, and Breton's group won the right to the term.

The movement was repeatedly divided over politics and membership, yet it spread to many countries and influenced Abstract Expressionism, the Beat writers, the Theatre of the Absurd and the French revolt of May 1968.
dyk: In 1938 the Paris Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme was lit only by a single light bulb over a coal brazier, with 1,200 coal bags hung from the ceiling, and visitors were given flashlights to view the art.
ev: Guillaume Apollinaire uses the word surrealism in his notes for the ballet Parade, which premiers on 18 May
Breton and Soupault publish The Magnetic Fields, written with automatic techniques
Yvan Goll publishes his Manifeste du surréalisme on 1 October and Breton publishes his on 15 October
La Peinture Surrealiste, the first Surrealist exhibition, is held at Galerie Pierre in Paris
The second Surrealist manifesto excludes members unwilling to commit to collective action, and the excluded respond with the pamphlet Un Cadavre
The London International Surrealist Exhibition is organised by Herbert Read, with an introduction by Breton
The Exposition Internationale du Surréalisme opens at the Beaux-arts Gallery in Paris, and the Chilean group La Mandrágora is founded
André Breton dies, and Surrealist groups continue without him

f.where: Paris was the most important centre; autonomous groups in Brussels and London, a second English group in Birmingham, Chile, Japan and Martinique; from the 1930s the idea spread to North America, South America, Central America, the Caribbean and Asia, and in the 1940s New York became a place of exile
f.period: the word coined by Guillaume Apollinaire in 1917; Dada years after the First World War; manifestos of October 1924; expansion in the mid-1920s; the 1930s described as a golden age; exile and the Second World War; Breton's return to France after the war; death of Breton in 1966; groups still active today
f.figures: André Breton, leader of the Paris group and author of the manifestos; Louis Aragon, Paul Éluard and Benjamin Péret, writers; Max Ernst, Joan Miró, André Masson and Yves Tanguy, painters; Salvador Dalí and René Magritte, who created the most widely recognised images of the movement; Man Ray, photographer; Luis Buñuel, film-maker; Yvan Goll, leader of a rival faction
f.outcome: Breton's group won the right to the name in 1924 but the movement was marked by fractures, resignations and expulsions; its ideas passed into Abstract Expressionism, the Beat writers, the Theatre of the Absurd and the events of May 1968, and Surrealist groups continue to publish and exhibit
